title: What Does ‘He Will Make Your Paths Straight’ Mean?
subtitle: Proverbs 3:5-6 is a father's counsel to his son. It promises a life made upright, not a map of the road ahead, and the same paragraph warns of the LORD's discipline.

sections.title: A Verse for Thresholds
sections.body:
This is a verse people give each other at thresholds. It is printed inside graduation cards and framed above office desks, written on the flyleaf of a Bible handed to a teenager, taped to a mirror in the month after a layoff or a diagnosis. Plenty of people who grew up in church could say it before they could find it: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5-6).

People love it for good reasons. It speaks to the moment when you can't see around the next bend, and it tells you that you don't have to. It asks for the whole heart, which is the only kind of trust worth giving, and it ends with a promise that God is not indifferent to the road you walk. A grandmother who writes it in the front of a grandchild's Bible is doing something the father in Proverbs 3 would recognize at once. She is handing wisdom down.

Still, the way the verse is usually heard has drifted from the way it was first spoken. On the card it tends to mean that if you trust God, He'll show you which way to go, as if the promise were a map revealed one decision at a time. Sometimes it means you should stop overthinking and just believe, and sometimes that things will work out if you trust Him. A skeptic who has watched Christians use it all three ways is right to say that we have. Reckless decisions have been dressed up as refusing to lean on our own understanding, and people in real pain have been told, sometimes in so many words, that the road turned rough because they didn't trust enough.

The verse can bear the weight people put on it. It just carries that weight differently than the card suggests, and the only way to see how is to read it where it sits.

sections.title: A Father Talking to His Son
sections.body:
Proverbs opens under the name of “Solomon son of David, king of Israel” (1:1), who reigned in the tenth century before Christ, and the book is candid that it grew over time. Some of Solomon's proverbs “were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah” (25:1) two centuries later, and scholars still debate when the first nine chapters reached their final form.

Who is speaking, and to whom, is not in doubt. Chapters 1 to 9 are mostly a father's speeches to his son: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother” (1:8). Chapter 3 alone uses the address three times (3:1, 3:11, 3:21), and a chapter later the father says he is passing on what his own father taught him (4:3-4). I was raised without a father, and I have five sons, so I can't read that as background. Proverbs 3:5-6 is what a father says to a young man about to choose his friends, his work, his marriage, and whether he will fear the LORD.

It is also wisdom literature, and wisdom speaks in general truths about how life under God tends to go rather than in guarantees. The book makes the point itself when it sets “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” beside “Answer a fool according to his folly” (26:4-5) and trusts the reader to know which one the moment calls for.

The paragraph around the verse, Proverbs 3:1-12, is built from six pairs, each a command followed by what comes of it: keep my teaching and live long, hold to loving devotion and find favor, trust the LORD and walk straight paths, fear Him and find healing, honor Him with your wealth and see full barns. The sixth pair turns the pattern over: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke; for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (3:11-12). The father who promised straight paths also told his son to expect the LORD's rebuke. Any honest reading of verse 6 has to make room for verse 12.

sections.title: What the Son Was Promised
sections.body:
The verse asks for all your heart, and in Proverbs the heart is where a person thinks, weighs, and plans: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (16:9). To trust the LORD with all your heart is to bring your planning mind to Him along with everything else.

So the next line can't be an instruction to stop thinking. Fourteen verses later the father says “The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding” (3:19), and again and again he begs his son to “gain understanding” (4:7). What he warns against is leaning on your own understanding, making it the ground you stand on and the last word you hear. Verse 7 names the fault: “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil.” The opposite of trust, in Proverbs, is not thought. It is self-trust.

The word translated “acknowledge” is the ordinary Hebrew verb for knowing. In all your ways, know Him: at the city gate and in the field, in what you do with your money (3:9) and how you treat the neighbor next door (3:29). Tremper Longman describes wisdom in Israel as practical, a skill for living; ethical, because the wise person is a good one; and most deeply theological, because it begins in the fear of the LORD. Verses 5 to 7 are that theological root, and every piece of practical advice in the book grows from it.

As for the promise, a straight path in Proverbs is an upright one. The Hebrew behind “straight” shares its root with the book's word for “the upright” (2:7), and the father warns his son away from “those who leave the straight paths to walk in the ways of darkness” (2:13). When he pictures how the promise comes true, he describes a sunrise: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday” (4:18). The son was promised a life made level and upright over years of walking with God, with the light growing as he went.

sections.title: What It Promises, and What It Does Not
sections.body:
The New Testament has already read this paragraph to a struggling church. The letter to the Hebrews was written to believers who had lost standing and property for their faith (10:32-34) and were growing tired. It tells them to fix their eyes on Jesus, “who for the joy set before Him endured the cross” (12:2), quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 to them, and then echoes the father in Proverbs 4:26: “Make straight paths for your feet” (12:13). In Hebrews, then, straight paths belong to people enduring hardship behind a crucified and risen Lord. That is what the verse still promises: a life God keeps setting right and turning toward Himself, through discipline and loss as well as good days.

What it does not promise is a map. The verse will not tell you which job to take or which city to move to, and Proverbs never expected it to. The same book says “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed” (15:22). It expects you to think, ask, weigh, and decide in the fear of the LORD, and then to trust Him with steps you can't see.

Nor does it promise a smooth road. Derek Kidner hears Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes as distinct voices that, taken together, give one view of life. Read alone, the proverbs can harden into guarantees. Beside Job, a man “blameless and upright” (Job 1:1) whose friends explained his suffering as punishment and were rebuked by God for it (Job 42:7), they cannot. Proverbs knows this too: “Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a rich man whose ways are perverse” (28:6).

Two misreadings grow from different soil and share one root. Where success is taken as proof of God's favor, verse 6 gets set beside verse 10 and the chapter becomes a transaction, trust and giving in exchange for a prosperous road. Where feelings are taken as guidance, the verse is heard as permission to trust your own heart, and God is asked to bless the road the heart had already chosen. Pastors, and I am one, are tempted by both, because both are easier to preach than verse 12. Both leave the self at the center of the verse. The verse puts God there, and the straight path is what happens to a person who knows Him.

sections.title: Praying It Without a Map
sections.body:
Pray it, then, for what it offers. Instead of asking God to show you the whole road, ask Him to teach you to know Him on the stretch you're on: in the job you already have, the money in your account, the marriage that is harder than you expected, the grief that hasn't lifted. Do your thinking, and do it with other people. Get counsel, weigh it, decide, and then trust Him with what you could not have known.

When hardship comes and feels like abandonment, don't take the feeling for the verdict. The father in Proverbs set the LORD's rebuke inside His delight (3:12), and Hebrews tells a weary church that hardship received as discipline means “God is treating you as sons” (12:7). Job stands guard against anyone who uses that sentence to explain a particular loss. What the sentence forbids is the conclusion we reach most easily in the dark: that God has gone.

And if you give this verse to a graduate, which is a fine thing to do, give it the way the father did, with the rest of the paragraph attached. The straightest path ever walked belonged to the Son who trusted His Father with all His heart, and it ran through Gethsemane and a cross before it ran out of an empty tomb. The verse will not show you the road ahead. It gives you a Father for all of it, and it asks for your whole heart in return.
